chapterTitle: Diencephalon, Reticular Formation, Sleep and Epilepsy

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The basal surface of tanycytes has:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and hypothalamic nuclei, allowing them to transport substances between the CSF and blood/hypothalamus. This makes them specialized for neuroendocrine communication.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes have basal processes for transport between ventricle and hypothalamus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tanycytes line which of the following:
questions.explanation: Tanycytes are specialized ependymal cells that line the third ventricle and other ventricular surfaces, particularly in the hypothalamus. They have long basal processes that extend to blood vessels and are involved in neuroendocrine regulation.
questions.keyConcept: Tanycytes: specialized ependymal cells lining 3rd ventricle, transport molecules between brain and CSF.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the hypothalamus:
options: Heat gain center is present in the anterior hypothalamus.
Ventromedial nuclei synchronize body activities according to dark-light cycles.
Posterior hypothalamus function as a sleep center.
Anterior hypothalamic nuclei play a role in all of sleep, heat loss, parasympathetic activity and sexual drive.
questions.explanation: Heat gain center is in the POSTERIOR hypothalamus (not anterior). Anterior hypothalamus is for heat loss. Satiety center (ventromedial) does not have intrinsic activity - it responds to signals. Suprachiasmatic nucleus regulates circadian rhythms, not body activities synchronization in that context.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior hypothalamus: heat loss. Posterior hypothalamus: heat gain. Ventromedial: satiety. Lateral: feeding.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT.
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has 4 layers (stratum zonale, stratum cinereum, stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci), not 5. The stratum basilare (basal layer) is not a recognized layer of the superior colliculus. It is part of the visual reflex pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers (superficial to deep): zonale → cinereum → opticum → lemnisci. Not stratum basilare.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The lateral ventricles are connected to the third ventricle via:
questions.explanation: The interventricular foramina of Monro connect each lateral ventricle to the third ventricle, allowing CSF flow between these chambers.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral to third ventricle: interventricular foramina of Monro.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Gracile tract:
options: Its sacral fibers are most lateral.
Originates from neurons of lamina I.
Terminates in ventral posterior lateral nucleus of thalamus (VPMN).
questions.explanation: The gracile tract conveys proprioceptive and fine touch sensations from the lower half of the body. It carries impulses from T7 spinal segment and below, with its fibers passing medially to the cuneate tract.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract carries proprioception from lower body

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with dilated lateral and third ventricles on brain imaging. Which structure is most likely obstructed?
options: Central canal of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: Obstructive hydrocephalus at the level of the foramen of Monro would cause dilation of the lateral and third ventricles but not the fourth ventricle (which would be normal size).
questions.keyConcept: Foramen of Monro obstruction causes dilation of lateral and third ventricles with normal fourth ventricle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei relays auditory impulses?
questions.explanation: The medial geniculate body is a thalamic relay nucleus for auditory information. It receives input from the inferior colliculus via the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects via acoustic radiation to the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. The lateral geniculate body relays visual impulses, not auditory.
questions.keyConcept: Medial geniculate body relays auditory impulses from inferior colliculus to auditory cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards the medial longitudinal bundle, choose the CORRECT statement:
options: It extends from thalamus to spinal cord.
In spinal cord, it is formed of ascending & descending tracts.
Its ascending fibers project to motor nuclei of cranial nerves III, IV & V.
Its descending fibers include tectospinal fibers.
Its ascending fibers are connected with interstitial nucleus of Cajal.
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal fasciculus runs in the brainstem and receives input from the vestibular nuclei, interstitial nucleus of Cajal, and the superior colliculus. It coordinates head and eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: MLF connects vestibular nuclei with eye movement nuclei

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Second order neuron in pain, temperature start in ......., go via ...........
questions.explanation: Second order neurons for pain/temperature start in the substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) of the posterior horn and ascend via the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Pain second order neuron

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tactile discrimination is characterized by:
options: It is tested through pin prick test.
Perceived at the level of the thalamus.
questions.explanation: Tactile discrimination (two-point discrimination) uses rapidly adapting receptors like Meissner's corpuscles to detect texture and shape, tested by ability to distinguish two close points.
questions.keyConcept: Tactile discrimination: rapidly adapting sensation tested by two-point discrimination.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Blockage of CSF flow between the 3rd & 4th ventricles involves the:
questions.explanation: The cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius is a narrow channel穿过 midbrain connecting the 3rd and 4th ventricles. Blockage of CSF flow between these ventricles occurs at the aqueduct, causing aqueductal stenosis and non-communicating hydrocephalus. The interventricular foramen connects lateral to 3rd ventricle; foramina of Magendie and Luschka connect 4th ventricle to subarachnoid space.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius connects 3rd and 4th ventricles; blockage causes non-communicating hydrocephalus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The analgesia system includes:
options: Raphe magnus nucleus in the post horn of the spinal cord.
The peri-aqueductal area in the mid-brain.
questions.explanation: The analgesia system includes the periaqueductal grey matter in the midbrain and the raphe magnus nucleus in the medulla, which modulate pain transmission through descending inhibitory pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Analgesia system: periaqueductal area in midbrain, raphe magnus in medulla.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Reappearance of the grasp reflex occurs in lesion of:
questions.explanation: Area 6 (premotor area) lies anterior to the primary motor cortex. Lesions here cause reappearance of primitive reflexes like the grasp reflex, as this area normally has an inhibitory influence on these reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Area 6 lesion causes return of grasp reflex

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The structure derived from the intermaxillary segment is the:
options: Lateral part of the upper lip.
Lateral part of the lower lip.
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (also called the primary palate) is formed by the fusion of the two medial nasal prominences. It gives rise to the philtrum of the upper lip, the primary palate (prem axilla), and the four incisor teeth. The lateral parts of the upper lip come from maxillary prominences.
questions.keyConcept: Intermaxillary segment (fused medial nasal prominences) forms the philtrum of upper lip, primary palate, and incisor teeth.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: After the age of 2 years, the anterior fontanelle is ossified to form:
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle (soft spot) is located at the junction of the sagittal and coronal sutures and normally closes by 18-24 months of age, forming the BREMA. The pterion is the H-shaped suture junction between frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid bones. The lambda is the junction of sagittal and lambdoid sutures; the inion is the external occipital protuberance.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior fontanelle ossifies to form BREMA (junction of sagittal and coronal sutures); closes by 18-24 months.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following is a part of the middle cranial fossa?
questions.explanation: The middle cranial fossa is bounded anteriorly by the lesser wing of the sphenoid, posteriorly by the petrous temporal ridge and dorsum sellae. The floor is formed by the greater wing of the sphenoid and the squamous temporal bone. The BODY of the sphenoid (containing the sella turcica) is part of the middle cranial fossa. The crista galli and cribriform plate are part of the anterior cranial fossa; the clivus is part of the posterior cranial fossa.
questions.keyConcept: Body of sphenoid is part of middle cranial fossa; houses pituitary gland in sella turcica.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of food accumulation and dripping from the side of his mouth, after recovering from a parotid surgery involving removal of the benign tumor. What is the most likely nerve involved.
questions.explanation: After parotid surgery, food accumulation and drooping from the side of the mouth indicates buccal nerve injury (a branch of the mandibular nerve, CN V3). The buccal nerve provides sensory innervation to the cheek mucosa and skin over the buccinator. Motor buccinator weakness (from CN VII) causes food accumulation, but after parotid surgery CN VII is at risk from the surgical field.
questions.keyConcept: Buccal nerve (sensory branch of CN V3) supplies cheek mucosa; post-parotid surgery causes buccal nerve injury with food accumulation and drooling.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The superior speech center is situated within the ……… area.
questions.explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA, medial area 6) is the superior speech center involved in planning and initiating speech movements, lying medial to premotor cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Superior speech center: supplementary motor area.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Inability to perform tasks although the person has the will to perform it indicates a lesion in ……… area.
questions.explanation: A premotor area lesion causes apraxia - inability to perform tasks despite intact motor pathways and will, due to loss of motor planning programs.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor lesion: apraxia (can't perform tasks despite will).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following mandibular ligaments is a remnant of cartilage of the 1st pharyngeal arch:
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament is the remnant of Meckel's cartilage (first pharyngeal arch cartilage), stretching from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible.
questions.keyConcept: Sphenomandibular ligament: remnant of 1st pharyngeal arch cartilage.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The inter-maxillary segment gives all the following EXCEPT:
options: Sockets of the upper 4 incisor teeth.
questions.explanation: The intermaxillary segment (primary palate) gives rise to the premaxilla, primary palate, and four incisor teeth. The center of the lower lip comes from the mandibular prominence, not the intermaxillary segment.
questions.keyConcept: Intermaxillary segment: premaxilla, primary palate, incisors (NOT secondary palate).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following ends in the VPMN of the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The nucleus solitarius (solitary nucleus) is the visceral afferent nucleus receiving general visceral afferent (GVA) and special visceral afferent (SVA - taste) fibers from CN VII, IX, and X.
questions.keyConcept: Nucleus solitarius - visceral afferent column

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The thalamic nucleus that relays pain and temperature sensations from the head is the:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus receives somatosensory input specifically from the head and face. It receives the trigeminal lemniscus (carrying pain, temperature, and touch from the face) and projects to the primary somatosensory cortex. VPL handles the body; VPM handles the face.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus relays pain, temperature, and touch sensations specifically from the HEAD and face.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Nucleus ventralis posterior medialis (VPM) of thalamus receives:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus receives the trigeminal lemniscus carrying pain, temperature, and touch sensation from the face and head. It also receives gustatory fibers from the nucleus solitarius. The medial lemniscus and spinal lemniscus terminate in VPL, not VPM.
questions.keyConcept: VPM receives trigeminal lemniscus (face sensation) and gustatory fibers from nucleus solitarius.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sensations received by the thalamus are Except:
questions.explanation: The thalamus receives exteroceptive, proprioceptive, gustatory, visual, and auditory sensations but NOT smell (olfactory). Olfaction is the only special sense that does not relay through the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Thalamus acts as sensory relay station for all senses except olfaction.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The frontal lobe of cerebral hemisphere DOESN'T include ……… area.
questions.explanation: The primary somatosensory area (postcentral gyrus, area 1-3) is in the parietal lobe, not the frontal lobe. Frontal lobe contains premotor, prefrontal, and Broca's areas.
questions.keyConcept: Frontal lobe doesn't include primary somatosensory (it's parietal).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterior cerebral artery supplies:
questions.explanation: PCA supplies: occipital lobe (visual cortex), lower border of temporal lobe, thalamus (central branches), and posterior limb of internal capsule; all of these are correct.
questions.keyConcept: PCA complete supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Central branches of posterior cerebral artery supply:
options: Posterior parts of caudate & lentiform nuclei
questions.explanation: Central branches of PCA (thalamogeniculate arteries) supply thalamus, lateral/genual geniculate bodies, and posterior parts of caudate and lentiform nuclei.
questions.keyConcept: PCA central branches

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: First order neuron in pain, temperature from head face is .............. while second order neuron is ..........
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature from the face: first order neurons are in the trigeminal (spinal) nucleus, second order are in the spinal trigeminal nucleus that projects to the thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Facial pain pathway

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: 24-year-old man was brought to the ER following a driving accident. Neurological testing revealed paraplegia and loss of all sensory modalities in bilateral lower limbs. Sensation for the upper limbs and the trunk was intact. Which of the following might be the nature and location of the lesion in this patient?
options: Complete section of spinal cord at C8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at C8 level
Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at T8 level
questions.explanation: The presentation of bilateral lower limb paralysis with intact upper limbs and trunk suggests central cord syndrome. Option C is correct because complete transection at T8 would paralyze everything below T8 (including trunk). Option E (central cord syndrome) is typically at C5-C6 levels and affects upper limbs more than lower due to the somatotopic arrangement of the corticospinal tract. The patient has paraplegia with intact upper limbs, which is most consistent with a T8 cord lesion where the corticospinal fibers for lower limbs are most affected.
questions.keyConcept: Central cord syndrome preferentially affects upper extremities due to the somatotopic organization of corticospinal fibers in the spinal cord.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei has a motor function?
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) thalamic nucleus is the primary motor relay nucleus. It receives input from the cerebellum (via dentatothalamic tract) and basal ganglia (via medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the motor cortex. It helps coordinate voluntary movement planning and execution.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the motor relay nucleus of the thalamus; receives cerebellar and basal ganglia input.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei relays motor impulses?
questions.explanation: The ventral anterior (VA) nucleus is a motor-related thalamic nucleus that receives input from the basal ganglia (via the medial globus pallidus internus) and projects to the premotor and motor cortices. It plays a role in motor planning and initiation. VA and VL together form the motor thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral anterior (VA) nucleus relays motor impulses from basal ganglia to motor cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The nucleus that projects neocerebellar efferent is the:
questions.explanation: The dentate nucleus is the main output nucleus of the neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres). It projects inhibitory fibers via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral thalamus (VPL/VPM) and red nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Dentate nucleus projects neocerebellar efferent

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar output:
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral thalamic nucleus receives input from the deep cerebellar nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose nuclei) via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract. It then projects to the motor and premotor cortices, serving as the cerebellar relay to the cerebrum.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar output to the cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The thalamic nucleus that relays cerebellar fibers to the cerebral cortex is the:
questions.explanation: The ventral lateral (VL) nucleus is the principal relay nucleus for cerebellar output destined for the cerebral cortex. It receives input from the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle and dentatothalamic tract, and projects to the motor and premotor cortices, influencing voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral lateral nucleus relays cerebellar fibers from the dentate nucleus to the motor cortex.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of which veins?
options: Right and left internal cerebral veins
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by the union of the two internal cerebral veins, which drain the deep brain structures including the basal ganglia and thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Vein of Galen forms from union of internal cerebral veins draining deep brain structures.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The thalamic nucleus for pain and temperature sensations of head is:
questions.explanation: The ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus is the specific relay center for pain, temperature, and crude touch sensations from the head (face, scalp, meninges, and oral cavity). It receives input from the spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve via the trigeminal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: VPM nucleus relays pain and temperature sensations specifically from the HEAD via trigeminal lemniscus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lemniscus of pathway from face and head called:
questions.explanation: The trigeminal lemniscus (trigeminothalamic tract) carries facial sensory information (touch, pain, temperature) from the principal sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei to the VPM thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal lemniscus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior external arcuate fibres relay in:
options: Arcuate nucleus of the same side.
Arcuate nucleus of the opposite side.
questions.explanation: Anterior external arcuate fibers relay in the arcuate nucleus of the opposite side before projecting to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior external arcuate relay

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which EEG wave pattern indicates deep (slow‑wave) sleep in an adult?
questions.explanation: Delta waves (0.5-2 Hz, high amplitude) are the hallmark of deep slow-wave sleep in adults, replacing alpha rhythms.
questions.keyConcept: Delta sleep waves

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is (are) included in the metathalamus:
questions.explanation: The metathalamus is the posterior part of the thalamus consisting of the medial and lateral geniculate bodies. The medial geniculate body relays auditory information; the lateral geniculate body relays visual information. The epithalamus (pineal body, habenular nuclei, posterior commissure) is a separate division.
questions.keyConcept: Metathalamus consists of medial and lateral geniculate bodies; relays auditory and visual impulses respectively.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Epithalamus is formed of:
questions.explanation: The epithalamus is the posterior portion of the thalamus comprising the pineal body, habenular nuclei, habenular commissure, and posterior commissure. It is involved in circadian rhythm regulation (via pineal melatonin secretion) and emotional processing related to the limbic system.
questions.keyConcept: Epithalamus comprises pineal body, habenular nuclei, and posterior commissure; regulates circadian rhythms.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following thalamic nuclei projects to the cingulate gyrus?
questions.explanation: The anterior thalamic nucleus is part of the limbic system's Papez circuit. It receives input from the hippocampus via the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus, which is involved in emotion, memory, and pain perception. This circuit is essential for emotional processing and memory consolidation.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior thalamic nucleus projects to cingulate gyrus as part of Papez limbic circuit.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding pituitary gland, all the following statements are true Except:
options: It lies in anterior part of the neck.
It has a portal system of veins.
Axons of nerve cells in hypothalamus carry hormones to the neurohypophysis.
The adenohypophysis secretes at least six different hormones.
questions.explanation: Pituitary gland: in sella turcica, connected to hypothalamus via infundibulum, anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis), has portal circulation.选项A正确. The answer is A. Portal system allows hypothalamic regulation.
questions.keyConcept: Pituitary: sella turcica, two lobes, portal circulation for hypothalamic control - posterior stores ADH/oxytocin.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following are efferent hypothalamic fibers Except:
questions.explanation: Corticohypothalamic fibers are afferent (going TO hypothalamus FROM cortex), not efferent. Efferent hypothalamic tracts include supraoptic hypophyseal, tuberoinfundibular, mamillotegmental, and paraventriculohypophyseal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamic efferent tracts: supraoptic-hypophyseal, tuberoinfundibular, mamillotegmental, paraventriculohypophyseal.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Stimulation of the lateral hypothalamic area in an experimental animal produces:
questions.explanation: The lateral hypothalamus is the feeding (hunger) center; stimulation produces hunger and eating behavior, while destruction causes anorexia.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral hypothalamus function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following shares in forming lateral wall of third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed superiorly by the thalamus and inferiorly by the hypothalamus, separated by the hypothalamic sulcus. The hypothalamus forms the floor and contributes to the anterior wall. The epithalamus forms the posterior wall. Lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall of 3rd ventricle is formed by thalamus (superior) and hypothalamus (inferior), separated by hypothalamic sulcus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed by:
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed superiorly by the thalamus and inferiorly by the hypothalamus, separated by the hypothalamic sulcus. Neither the lamina terminalis nor the anterior commissure forms the lateral wall; they are part of the anterior wall and intraventricular structures respectively.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral wall of 3rd ventricle is formed by thalamus (superior part) and hypothalamus (inferior part).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following shares in forming anterior wall of 3rd ventricle?
questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the third ventricle is formed by the lamina terminalis, which extends from the optic chiasma superiorly to the anterior commissure. The anterior columns of the fornix also contribute. The hypothalamus forms the floor, the thalamus forms the lateral wall, and the epithalamus (pineal body) forms the posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina terminalis forms the anterior wall of the third ventricle, connecting optic chiasma to anterior commissure.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following shares in forming the lateral wall of the third ventricle?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the third ventricle is formed by the thalamus (superior portion) and hypothalamus (inferior portion), separated by the hypothalamic sulcus. The epithalamus, lamina terminalis, anterior commissure, and habenular nuclei do not form the lateral wall—they are components of the anterior or posterior walls.
questions.keyConcept: Hypothalamus contributes to lateral wall of 3rd ventricle (inferior part); thalamus forms the superior part.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The inferior petrosal sinus connects the cavernous sinus with the:
questions.explanation: The cavernous part of the internal carotid artery gives off the inferolateral (暴发性) trunk and meningohypophyseal trunk branches, which supply the dura and pituitary gland.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous ICA gives meningohypophyseal trunk

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following foramina gives passage to emissary vein of the superior sagittal sinus?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus is related laterally to the temporal lobe of the brain and the greater wing of the sphenoid bone. Medially relations include the internal carotid artery and the pituitary gland.
questions.keyConcept: Cavernous sinus lateral relation is temporal lobe

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following structures does not contribute to floor of 3rd Ventricle:
questions.explanation: The floor of the third ventricle (from anterior to posterior) is formed by the optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, and posterior perforated substance. The lamina terminalis forms the AN anterior wall of the third ventricle, not the floor. The optic chiasma lies just above the pituitary stalk at the anterior aspect of the ventricle.
questions.keyConcept: Lamina terminalis forms anterior wall of 3rd ventricle, NOT the floor. Floor = optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A structure that forms the anterior wall of third ventricle:
questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the third ventricle is formed by the lamina terminalis (extends from the optic chiasma to the anterior commissure), the anterior column of the fornix, and the anterior commissure. The optic chiasma forms the inferiormost part of the anterior boundary. The pineal body forms the posterior wall.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior wall of 3rd ventricle = lamina terminalis + anterior column of fornix + anterior commissure.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: As regards boundaries of 3rd ventricle, choose INCORRECT matching:
questions.explanation: The third ventricle has the following boundaries: anterior wall = lamina terminalis; posterior wall = pineal body and posterior commissure; medial wall = thalamus (lateral wall) and hypothalamus; roof = choroid plexus and fornix body; floor = optic chiasma, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, posterior perforated substance. The medial wall is formed by the THALAMUS, not hypothalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Incorrect matching: medial wall of 3rd ventricle = thalamus, NOT hypothalamus. Floor = optic chiasma.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not common adverse effect of nitrous oxide:
options: Hypoxia if take pure without oxygen
Increase pressure in the middle ear
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide (N2O) side effects: A) Hypoxia if given pure - TRUE, must be given with at least 30% oxygen; B) Increased middle ear pressure - TRUE, N2O diffuses into middle ear 34x faster than nitrogen diffuses out, causing pressure increase; C) Abortion on prolonged exposure - TRUE, N2O inhibits methionine synthase and may affect reproduction; D) Hepatic toxicity - FALSE, N2O has minimal hepatic metabolism and is NOT hepatotoxic. Unlike halothane, N2O doesn't cause hepatitis or hepatic necrosis. This makes it safer for patients with liver disease. The correct answer is D.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide lacks hepatotoxicity unlike halogenated anesthetics, making it safer for patients with liver disease.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Ethosuximide is useful in:
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is the first-line treatment for absence seizures (petit mal) by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. It is not effective for partial epilepsy or tonic-clonic seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide: first-line for absence seizures (not partial or tonic-clonic)

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: An antiepileptic drug for absence seizures is:
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is the drug of choice for absence seizures. Option C is correct. Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, specifically effective for absence seizures. Diazepam (A) is for status epilepticus. Carbamazepine (B) and phenytoin (D) can worsen absence seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide's thalamic T-channel blockade specifically suppresses absence seizure activity.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following antiepileptic drug is not matched with its adverse effect
questions.explanation: Gabapentin does NOT cause megaloblastic anemia - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Gabapentin's adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema. Megaloblastic anemia is associated with phenytoin and carbamazepine (folate metabolism interference). Options A, C, D are correctly matched.
questions.keyConcept: Gabapentin is not associated with megaloblastic anemia; it causes dizziness, sedation, and edema.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: An antiepileptic drug for absence seizures is :
questions.explanation: Ethosuximide is specifically used for absence seizures. Diazepam (A) is used for status epilepticus, not absence maintenance therapy. Carbamazepine (B) is for partial seizures and can actually worsen absence seizures. Phenytoin (D) is for generalized tonic-clonic and partial seizures, not absence. Ethosuximide works by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. The answer is C - ethosuximide is the antiepileptic for absence seizures.
questions.keyConcept: Ethosuximide selectively treats absence seizures via T-type calcium channel blockade.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: How do general anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity?
options: They facilitate inhibitory effects of GABA at GABA receptors
Inhibit excitatory effects of glutamate at NMDA receptors
questions.explanation: General anesthetics inhibit neuronal activity by enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission (GABA-A receptor activation - barbiturates, benzodiazepines, propofol, isoflurane) or inhibiting excitatory neurotransmission (NMDA receptor blockade - ketamine, nitrous oxide).选项C正确. The answer is C. Some agents do both. The net effect is decreased neuronal excitability and consciousness.
questions.keyConcept: General anesthetics enhance GABA (inhibitory) or block NMDA (excitatory) to inhibit neuronal activity.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which combination of drugs should be avoided because both can cause agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation: Clozapine and carbamazepine both cause agranulocytosis; their combination dramatically increases this risk and is contraindicated.
questions.keyConcept: Agranulocytosis drug interaction

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The only medically justified long‑term use of phenobarbital is for:
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital is justified long-term only for certain epilepsies (generalized tonic-clonic, partial seizures) due to its side effect profile.
questions.keyConcept: Phenobarbital use

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which antiepileptic is used as migraine prophylaxis and can cause weight loss and renal stones?
questions.explanation: Topiramate is used for migraine prophylaxis and causes weight loss and renal calcium phosphate stones (carbonic anhydrase inhibition).
questions.keyConcept: Topiramate uses

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which statement about ester local anesthetics is false?
options: They are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases.
Procaine is a member of this group.
They are shorter acting than amides.
They are less liable to induce allergy.
They are less liable to systemic toxicity than amides.
questions.explanation: Ester local anesthetics are MORE liable to cause allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) metabolite, not less.
questions.keyConcept: Ester local anesthetic allergy

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following drug is not matched with its mechanism of action:
options: Diazepam increases frequency of opening of chloride channels
Zolpidem binds with BZD1 subtype that increases GABA activity
Barbiturates increase duration of opening of chloride channels
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A PARTIAL AGONIST, not antagonist. Option D incorrectly states 'selective 5HT1A antagonist' - this is wrong. Options A, B, C are correctly matched: A) Diazepam increases frequency of chloride channel opening (BZD mechanism); B) Zolpidem is BZD1-selective; C) Barbiturates increase duration of chloride channel opening. The correct answer is D because buspirone's mechanism is agonist (partial agonist) activity at 5-HT1A receptors, not antagonist. This partial agonist activity provides anxiolytic effects while having minimal sedative and dependence potential.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist, not antagonist - this distinguishes it from other anxiolytics.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which antiepileptic drug is associated with the highest risk of neonatal cleft lip and cleft palate?
questions.explanation: Phenytoin is associated with fetal hydantoin syndrome causing cleft lip/palate, digital hypoplasia, and growth retardation.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin teratogenicity

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Choose the Incorrect statement
options: Buspirone is selective anxiolytic with delayed onset of action
Ramelteon is selective melatonin receptors antagonist
Flumazenil is short acting BDZ receptor antagonist
Eszopiclone is intermediate acting non BDZ hypnotic
questions.explanation: Ramelteon is a melatonin RECEPTOR AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Ramelteon is a selective melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist used for insomnia. Options A, C, D are correct: buspirone is selective anxiolytic, flumazenil is BZD antagonist, eszopiclone is non-BZD hypnotic.
questions.keyConcept: Ramelteon works as a melatonin receptor agonist, not antagonist, to promote sleep.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following concerning the use of benzodiazepines is not true
options: Abuse is associated with memory loss.
Toxic dose results in prolonged sleep.
Respiratory depression is reversed by flumazenil.
Shorter acting agents are preferred as anxiolytics.
questions.explanation: Shorter acting agents are NOT preferred as anxiolytics - this is NOT true. Option D is incorrect. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) are preferred for anxiety because they provide steady plasma levels. Short-acting agents (triazolam) cause more rebound anxiety and are used for insomnia. Options A, B, C are correct: abuse causes memory loss, toxic dose causes prolonged sleep, flumazenil reverses respiratory depression.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred for anxiety due to stable plasma concentrations and reduced rebound effects.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: A drug whose toxic dose results in prolonged sleep reversed by flumazenil
questions.explanation: Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine; overdose causes prolonged sedation that is reversed by flumazenil. Barbiturates (like pentobarbital) are not reversed by flumazenil.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine overdose but not barbiturate overdose.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Gingival hyperplasia is a common side effect of:
questions.explanation: Gingival hyperplasia is a common side effect of phenytoin. Option B is correct. Phenytoin's well-known side effects include gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, coarse facial features, and osteomalacia. Valproate (A) causes weight gain, tremor, hepatotoxicity. Ethosuximide (C) causes GI upset, headache. Carbamazepine (D) causes SIADH, aplastic anemia.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and coarse facial features through effects on connective tissue.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following side effect is most likely to be seen with carbamazepine
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine causes WATER RETENTION (SIADH). Option A is correct. Carbamazepine induces SIADH, causing hyponatremia and water retention. Options B, C, D are phenytoin effects (coarse facial features, hirsutism, gingival hyperplasia).
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine's SIADH effect causes dilutional hyponatremia requiring monitoring.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Hirsutism may be induced by:
questions.explanation: Hirsutism may be induced by phenytoin. Option D is correct. Phenytoin causes hirsutism (excessive hair growth) as a characteristic side effect. Valproate (A) causes weight gain, tremor. Interferon (B) causes flu-like symptoms. Heparin (C) causes osteoporosis.
questions.keyConcept: Phenytoin causes hirsutism through altered androgen metabolism and connective tissue effects.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Valproate toxicity does not include:
questions.explanation: Hirsutism is NOT valproate toxicity - it is caused by phenytoin. Option A is incorrect. Valproate causes hand tremor, thrombocytopenia, hepatotoxicity (rare but fatal). Options B, C, D are valproate toxicities. Hirsutism is a phenytoin effect.
questions.keyConcept: Valproate's main toxicities include hepatotoxicity, thrombocytopenia, and tremor; hirsutism is a phenytoin effect.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Intrapartum Group B streptococcus prophylaxis requirements:
options: History of delivery of infant with GBS
History of GBS bacteriuria at any time during pregnancy
questions.explanation: All listed are established indications for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: GBS colonization, prior infant with GBS disease, and GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy all mandate intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.
questions.keyConcept: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis is indicated for colonization, prior affected infant, or GBS bacteriuria during pregnancy.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding Natalizumab?
options: Indicated in mild controlled Multiple sclerosis
questions.explanation: Natalizumab is indicated for aggressive or relapsing‑remitting MS with high disease activity, not for mild controlled disease. It is given as monthly IV infusion and is a monoclonal antibody against α4‑integrin.
questions.keyConcept: Natalizumab is reserved for aggressive, highly active MS rather than mild disease, and reduces lymphocyte CNS invasion.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following concerning the use of benzodiazepines is not true:
options: Abuse is associated with memory loss
Toxic dose results in prolonged sleep
Respiratory depression is reversed by Flumazenil
Shorter acting agent are preferred as anxiolytics
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepine properties: A) True - abuse causes memory impairment (anterograde amnesia); B) FALSE - toxic doses cause prolonged sleep but respiratory depression is minimal (BZD safety margin is high); C) True - flumazenil reverses respiratory depression; D) True - shorter-acting agents (alprazolam, oxazepam) are preferred for anxiety because long-acting agents accumulate. Option B is the wrong statement because BZDs have a wide safety margin - respiratory depression at toxic doses is less severe than with barbiturates or opioids. This is why BZD overdose rarely causes fatal respiratory depression alone.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines have a wide safety margin with minimal respiratory depression even in overdose.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is wrong statement about BZDs:
options: Lorazepam is an intermediate duration and effective anxiolytic and used in status epilepticus
Midazolam is long acting used in anesthesia as hypnotic and should be avoided as anxiolytic
Alprazolam is effective in controlling the panic attacks
Diazepam is long acting & useful during alcohol withdrawal
questions.explanation: Midazolam is SHORT-acting, not long-acting. This statement is incorrect: 'Midazolam is long acting used in anesthesia as hypnotic and should be avoided as anxiolytic.' Midazolam has rapid onset, short duration (~2 hours), and is actually USEFUL as an anxiolytic and sedative premedication. Options A, C, D are correct descriptions. Midazolam is commonly used for conscious sedation, induction of anesthesia, and status epilepticus due to its short action. The incorrect statement about midazolam being long-acting makes B the answer.
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam is short-acting, making it suitable for anxiolysis and procedural sedation, not something to avoid.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following side effect is most likely to be seen with carbamazepine:
questions.explanation: Phenytoin causes gingival hyperplasia (swollen, overgrown gums) - this is a well-known side effect requiring good dental hygiene. Carbamazepine causes: water retention/SIADH (not listed as side effect in options), coarse facial features (not typical), hirsutism (not typical), and aplastic anemia/agranulocytosis (blood dyscrasias). Among the options given, gingival hyperplasia is associated with phenytoin, not carbamazepine. Carbamazepine's side effects include: hyponatremia, aplastic anemia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, enzyme induction. The answer is D - gingival hyperplasia is most likely seen with phenytoin, not carbamazepine.
questions.keyConcept: Gingival hyperplasia is a classic side effect of phenytoin, not carbamazepine.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is not adverse effect of carbamazepine:
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine side effects: agranulocytosis (yes - blood dyscrasia), dilutional hyponatremia (yes - SIADH), enzyme inducer (yes - induces CYP450). questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes agranulocytosis, hyponatremia, and is an enzyme inducer; megaloblastic anemia is associated with phenytoin.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not adverse effect of lithium carbonate:
questions.explanation: Lithium carbonate side effects include: ataxia and tremors (CNS toxicity - A is a side effect), polyuria and thirst (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus - B is a side effect), renal tubular damage (nephrotoxicity with long-term use - D is a side effect). The answer is C - hypertension is not an adverse effect of lithium carbonate; actually the opposite (hypotension) occurs.
questions.keyConcept: Lithium causes hypotension, not hypertension, along with tremors, polyuria, and renal tubular damage.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: What are the therapeutic uses of anticholinergic drugs?
questions.explanation: Anticholinergic drugs therapeutic uses in PD: control of tremor and rigidity (not bradykinesia), drooling, excessive salivation, and oily skin. They work by blocking muscarinic receptors in the striatum, reducing cholinergic activity that becomes relatively increased in PD.选项C正确. The answer is C. Anticholinergics are less effective for bradykinesia and are now second-line due to side effects.
questions.keyConcept: Anticholinergics treat PD tremor and rigidity by blocking excess cholinergic activity in the striatum.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which drug can be used to control tremors in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia?
questions.explanation: Propranolol (beta-blocker) effectively controls essential tremor and is safe in BPH patients.
questions.keyConcept: Essential tremor in BPH

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: What are the extrapyramidal adverse effects of antipsychotics?
questions.explanation: Extrapyramidal effects of antipsychotics: acute dystonia, akathisia (restlessness), parkinsonism (bradykinesia, rigidity, tremor), and tardive dyskinesia (late-onset choreiform movements).选项D正确. The answer is D. Caused by D2 blockade in nigrostriatal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: EPS includes acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia from nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is a wrong statement about therapy of Parkinson’s disease
options: High protein diet is not recommended in the same time with L- dopa administration
Multivitamin including vitamin B6 is recommended to improve general condition of the patient
Diet rich in fibers is useful to minimize constipation especially if the patient on Benztropine therapy.
A Beta blocker may be added in the therapy to control tremors
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 is NOT recommended - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Pyridoxine (B6) enhances peripheral decarboxylation of L-dopa, reducing its CNS availability. High protein diet reduces L-dopa absorption (correct). Fiber-rich diet helps constipation (correct). Beta-blockers can help tremors (correct).
questions.keyConcept: Pyridoxine (B6) should be avoided in patients taking L-dopa as it accelerates peripheral metabolism of the drug.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Uses of antiepileptics include all the following Except:
options: Lamotrigine / mood stabilizer in bipolar manic depression

Carbamazepine causes syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), leading to hyponatremia. Options A, B, C are correct: lamotrigine is mood stabilizer, phenytoin treats digitalis arrhythmias, gabapentin treats neuropathic pain.
questions.keyConcept: Carbamazepine causes SIADH with water retention and hyponatremia, requiring monitoring.
